subtopics.title: Alternating Current Fundamentals
subtopics.subtitle: Sinusoidal waveform, period, frequency, angular frequency, phase and phasors

concepts.text: Alternating Current versus Direct Current

Direct current (DC) flows in one direction only and, from a battery, has a constant magnitude. Alternating current (AC) reverses its direction periodically and its magnitude changes continuously with time, so its average over a complete cycle is zero. Power stations generate AC because a coil rotating at constant speed in a uniform magnetic field naturally produces a sinusoidal EMF, and this sine shape is preserved through transformers and linear circuits. The Nepal mains supply is single-phase 230 V, 50 Hz AC, taken from a 400 V three-phase distribution network.
Sinusoidal Quantities

An AC voltage v(t) = Vm sin(2πft) is described by its peak value Vm, its frequency f and its period T = 1/f. Writing ω = 2πf, the general form is v = Vm sin(ωt + φ), where φ is the phase angle at t = 0. The value of v at any chosen instant is the instantaneous value; Vm is the amplitude, the largest instantaneous value reached. Two derived values also matter for exams: the average and the RMS value, covered in the next subtopic.

concepts.latex: v = V_m\sin(\omega t + \phi),\qquad i = I_m\sin(\omega t + \phi_i)
concepts.plainText: v = Vm sin(ωt + φ),  i = Im sin(ωt + φi)

concepts.text: Terms in the equation:
items: Instantaneous value v or i: the value at a particular instant t; it swings between +Vm and −Vm.
Amplitude or peak value Vm, Im: the maximum instantaneous value.
Angular frequency ω = 2πf, in rad/s: the rate at which the angle ωt advances.
Phase angle φ, in degrees or radians: the shift of the wave from the reference at t = 0.
ωt is in radians; convert to degrees (multiply by 180/π) before adding a phase angle given in degrees.

concepts.text: Derived values (details in Peak, Average and RMS Values):
items: RMS (root mean square) value produces the same heating effect as an equal DC value.
Average value is taken over a half cycle (the full-cycle average of a sine is zero).
Form factor = RMS / Average = 1.11 for a sine wave.
Peak (crest) factor = Peak / RMS = 1.414 for a sine wave.

concepts.text: Cycle, Time Period and Frequency

One cycle is one complete positive and one complete negative half cycle, after which the waveform repeats; in angle it spans 360° or 2π radians. The time period T is the time taken for one cycle, in seconds. Frequency f is the number of cycles completed per second, in hertz (Hz), so f = 1/T. Angular frequency ω = 2π/T = 2πf, in rad/s, is the angle swept per second by the rotating phasor that generates the wave. For the 50 Hz supply, T = 1/50 = 20 ms and ω = 2π × 50 = 314.16 rad/s.

concepts.plainText: f = 1/T,  ω = 2πf = 2π/T

concepts.text: Phase Difference and Phasors

Two sinusoids of the same frequency generally do not pass through zero at the same instant; the angle between corresponding zero crossings (or peaks) is their phase difference. With v = Vm sin ωt as reference, a current i = Im sin(ωt − φ) reaches its peak later and is said to lag the voltage by φ, while i = Im sin(ωt + φ) peaks earlier and leads by φ. A time displacement Δt corresponds to a phase angle φ = ωΔt = 360° × Δt/T. Phase difference has meaning only between quantities of the same frequency.
Phase relationships:
items: In phase (φ = 0): both waves pass through zero and peak together, as voltage and current in a pure resistor.
Lagging: the current peaks after the voltage, as in an inductive circuit (90° for a pure inductor).
Leading: the current peaks before the voltage, as in a capacitive circuit (90° for a pure capacitor).
Quadrature: 90° apart. Antiphase: 180° apart, so one wave is the negative of the other.

concepts.text: A sinusoid of fixed frequency is completely specified by its magnitude and phase, so it can be represented by a phasor: an arrow whose length is the RMS (or peak) value and whose angle from the reference axis is the phase angle, imagined rotating anticlockwise at ω rad/s. The projection of the rotating arrow on the vertical axis traces out the sine wave. Sinusoids of the same frequency are added by adding their phasors like vectors, which replaces lengthy trigonometry; the angle between two phasors is their phase difference, and the phasor further anticlockwise leads.
Why AC is used for generation and transmission:
items: Alternators are simpler and cheaper than DC generators: no commutator, so very high voltages and large ratings are possible.
Transformers work only with AC, so the voltage is stepped up for transmission (less current, less I²R loss, thinner conductors) and stepped down for safe use.
AC induction motors are rugged, self-starting (three-phase) and need little maintenance.
AC is easy to interrupt because the current passes through zero twice every cycle.
AC is readily converted to DC by rectifiers wherever DC is needed (electronics, electroplating, battery charging).

rows: High voltage, low loss; reactance and skin effect present
No reactance; HVDC only for very long lines
Harder: the arc must be forced to zero

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Sinusoids and Phasor Algebra

Before two sinusoids can be compared, both must be written in the same function with a positive amplitude. A cosine is a sine advanced by 90°, so cos ωt = sin(ωt + 90°), and a negative amplitude is the same as a 180° shift, so −sin ωt = sin(ωt ± 180°). Only after this rewriting can the phase angles be subtracted to give the phase difference. For example, i = 5 cos(ωt − 30°) is really 5 sin(ωt + 60°), so it leads v = 10 sin(ωt + 20°) by 40°, not lags it by 50°.

concepts.plainText: cos ωt = sin(ωt + 90°),  −sin ωt = sin(ωt ± 180°)

concepts.text: The sum of two sinusoids of the same frequency is always another sinusoid of that frequency. Writing each as a phasor and resolving it into a horizontal component (A cos α) and a vertical component (A sin α), the components simply add. The resultant magnitude follows from Pythagoras, or directly from the cosine rule applied to the two phasors, and its angle θ from tan θ = (A sin α + B sin β)/(A cos α + B cos β), the ratio of the vertical to the horizontal sum. Subtraction is done by reversing the phasor to be subtracted (adding 180° to its angle) and then adding.

concepts.plainText: R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos(α − β))

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: add i1 = 10 sin ωt and i2 = 20 sin(ωt + 60°) A
Horizontal sum: 10 cos 0° + 20 cos 60° = 10 + 10 = 20
Vertical sum:   10 sin 0° + 20 sin 60° = 0 + 17.32 = 17.32
Magnitude:      R = √(20² + 17.32²) = √700 = 26.46 A
Angle:          θ = tan⁻¹(17.32/20) = 40.9°
Result:         i = 26.46 sin(ωt + 40.9°) A
Check with the cosine rule: √(100 + 400 + 2·10·20·cos 60°) = √700  (same)
Note: the arithmetic sum 30 A would be correct only if the currents were in phase.

Worked example 2: v = 200 sin(100πt) V, a 50 Hz wave
(a) Value at t = 4 ms: angle = 100π × 0.004 = 0.4π rad = 72°
    v = 200 sin 72° = 190.2 V
(b) First time v reaches +100 V: sin θ = 100/200 = 0.5, θ = π/6 rad
    t = θ/ω = (π/6)/(100π) = 1/600 s = 1.67 ms
(c) Next time v = +100 V (falling): θ = π − π/6 = 5π/6
    t = (5π/6)/(100π) = 1/120 s = 8.33 ms
Calculator in degree mode for (a) would wrongly give 200 sin(1.257°) = 4.4 V.

concepts.latex: r = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2},\; \theta = \tan^{-1}(b/a),\; a = r\cos\theta,\; b = r\sin\theta
concepts.plainText: r = √(a² + b²), θ = tan⁻¹(b/a), a = r cos θ, b = r sin θ

concepts.text: Three special cases save time. In-phase phasors add arithmetically (R = A + B); antiphase phasors subtract (R = |A − B|, taking the angle of the larger); phasors in quadrature combine by Pythagoras (R = √(A² + B²)). The operator j rotates a phasor 90° anticlockwise without changing its length, j² = −1 is a 180° rotation, and dividing by j rotates it 90° clockwise. In polar form, multiplication multiplies magnitudes and adds angles, while division divides magnitudes and subtracts angles.
Common mistakes in sinusoid and phasor problems:
items: Adding peak magnitudes of phasors that are not in phase; magnitudes add only when the angles are equal.
Comparing a sine with a cosine, or a wave with a negative amplitude, without first converting both to positive-amplitude sines.
Evaluating sin(ωt) with the calculator in degree mode while ωt is in radians.
Using tan⁻¹(b/a) blindly when a is negative; the angle must be placed in the correct quadrant (add 180°).
Mixing RMS and peak lengths in one phasor diagram; use one convention for every phasor.
Quoting a phase difference between waves of different frequencies, which keeps changing with time.

concepts.text: For a sum like A sin ωt + B cos ωt, write the answer at once as √(A² + B²) sin(ωt + tan⁻¹(B/A)); for example 30 sin ωt + 40 cos ωt = 50 sin(ωt + 53.13°).

notes.text: For 50 Hz mains remember T = 20 ms and ω = 2π × 50 = 314.16 rad/s; both appear directly in one-mark questions. Doubling the frequency halves the period and doubles ω.

In v = Vm sin(ωt + φ) the product ωt is in radians. Either keep the calculator in radian mode or convert with 180/π before adding a phase angle given in degrees; mixing the two units is the most common error in instantaneous-value questions.
Lead and lag are relative statements: if the current lags the voltage by 30°, the voltage leads the current by 30°. A negative phase angle in the equation of a quantity means it lags the reference.
Phase difference is defined only between sinusoids of the same frequency. Given a time shift Δt, the phase shift is 360° × Δt/T, so a 5 ms shift at 50 Hz is 90°.

formulas.title: Instantaneous value of AC
formulas.description: Instantaneous voltage v at time t from peak value Vm, angular frequency ω = 2πf and phase angle φ; the same form gives i = Im sin(ωt + φ).

formulas.title: Frequency and time period
formulas.description: Frequency f in hertz is the reciprocal of the time period T in seconds; 50 Hz corresponds to T = 20 ms.

formulas.title: Angular frequency
formulas.description: Angular frequency ω in rad/s from frequency f or period T; equals 314.16 rad/s for 50 Hz.

formulas.title: Phase angle from time shift
formulas.description: Converts a time displacement Δt between two waves of period T into a phase difference φ; use 360° for degrees or ω for radians.

If v = Vm sin ωt and i = Im sin(ωt − 30°), does the current lead or lag?

questions.questionText: The mains supply in Nepal has a frequency of 50 Hz. Its time period and angular frequency are:
A voltage is given by v = 100 sin(314t + 30°) V. Its instantaneous value at t = 0 is:
questions.explanation: At t = 0 the angle is just the phase angle, so v = 100 sin 30° = 100 × 0.5 = 50 V.

questions.questionText: In an AC circuit v = Vm sin ωt and i = Im sin(ωt − π/3). The phase relationship between current and voltage is:
options: Current and voltage are in phase
questions.explanation: π/3 rad = 60°, and the negative sign means the current reaches its peak later than the voltage, so it lags by 60° (an inductive circuit).

questions.questionText: In a 50 Hz circuit the current reaches its positive peak 2.5 ms after the voltage reaches its positive peak. The phase difference is:
questions.explanation: T = 20 ms, so φ = 360° × Δt/T = 360° × 2.5/20 = 45°. The current peaks later than the voltage, so it lags.

questions.questionText: An alternating voltage has a time period of 2.5 ms. Its frequency is:
The angular frequency of a 60 Hz supply is approximately:
questions.explanation: ω = 2πf = 2π × 60 = 377 rad/s. Omitting the factor 2 gives 188.5 rad/s.

questions.questionText: The frequency of the voltage v = 150 sin(628t) V is approximately:
questions.explanation: The coefficient of t is ω = 628 rad/s, so f = ω/2π = 628/6.283 ≈ 100 Hz.

questions.questionText: The frequency of an alternating quantity is defined as:
options: The time taken to complete one cycle
The angle swept per second by its phasor
The maximum value reached in one cycle
The number of cycles completed per second
questions.explanation: Frequency is cycles per second (hertz). The time for one cycle is the period T, the angle per second is ω, and the maximum value is the amplitude.

questions.questionText: One complete cycle of a sinusoidal waveform corresponds to an angle of:
questions.explanation: A full cycle (one positive and one negative half cycle) spans 360°, which is 2π radians.

questions.questionText: The SI unit of angular frequency ω is:
questions.explanation: ω = 2πf is the angle in radians swept per second, so its unit is rad/s; hertz is the unit of f.

questions.questionText: When a sinusoidal voltage is applied to a pure resistor, the current is:
questions.explanation: In a resistor i = v/R at every instant, so the current passes through zero and peaks at the same instants as the voltage.

questions.questionText: Two sinusoidal voltages of the same frequency differ in phase by 180°. They are said to be:
options: Out of step by one cycle
questions.explanation: A 180° difference means one wave is the negative of the other (antiphase); 90° is quadrature and 0° is in phase.

questions.questionText: The value of an alternating quantity at a particular instant of time is called its:
questions.explanation: The instantaneous value v or i is the value at a chosen instant t; the peak is the largest of these values.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of AC over DC?
options: AC can be stored directly in batteries
AC voltage can be changed easily with transformers
AC is easier to interrupt because the current passes through zero
questions.explanation: Batteries store energy only as DC; AC must be rectified before charging a battery. The other three are genuine advantages of AC.

questions.questionText: On a phasor diagram with phasors rotating anticlockwise, phasor A is drawn at 50° and phasor B at 20° from the reference axis. Which statement is correct?
options: A and B are in quadrature
questions.explanation: With anticlockwise rotation, the phasor further anticlockwise leads; A is 50° − 20° = 30° ahead of B.

questions.questionText: A 50 Hz sinusoidal voltage passes through zero how many times in one second?
questions.explanation: A sine wave crosses zero twice per cycle, so the number of zero crossings per second is 2f = 2 × 50 = 100.

questions.questionText: A voltage v = 200 sin(314t) V. Its instantaneous value at t = 2 ms is approximately:
questions.explanation: ωt = 314 × 0.002 = 0.628 rad = 36°, so v = 200 sin 36° = 117.5 V. Using degree mode on 0.628 gives the wrong 2.19 V.

questions.questionText: For v = 100 sin(100πt) V, the first instant after t = 0 at which v equals 86.6 V is:
questions.explanation: sin θ = 86.6/100 = 0.866 gives θ = π/3 rad, so t = θ/ω = (π/3)/(100π) = 1/300 s = 3.33 ms. 6.67 ms is the second instant, on the falling side.

questions.questionText: A current i = 10 sin(2π × 50 t) A starts at zero at t = 0. It first reaches its positive peak at:
questions.explanation: The first peak occurs a quarter cycle after the positive-going zero: T/4 = 20 ms/4 = 5 ms.

questions.questionText: Two 50 Hz sinusoids have a phase difference of 72°. The corresponding time displacement between them is:
Given va = 10 sin(ωt + 20°) and vb = 5 cos(ωt − 30°), the correct phase relationship is:
questions.explanation: vb = 5 cos(ωt − 30°) = 5 sin(ωt − 30° + 90°) = 5 sin(ωt + 60°). The difference is 60° − 20° = 40°, with vb ahead.

questions.questionText: The current i = −20 sin(ωt − 30°) A can be written with a positive amplitude as:
questions.explanation: A negative sign is a 180° shift: −20 sin(ωt − 30°) = 20 sin(ωt − 30° + 180°) = 20 sin(ωt + 150°) A.

questions.questionText: Two sinusoidal voltages of the same frequency, with peak values 5 V and 12 V, are in quadrature. The peak value of their sum is:
questions.explanation: For phasors 90° apart, R = √(5² + 12²) = √169 = 13 V; 17 V would apply only if they were in phase.

questions.questionText: Two currents i1 = 8 sin ωt A and i2 = 6 sin(ωt + 180°) A flow into a junction. The resultant current is:
questions.explanation: The phasors are in antiphase, so they subtract: 8 − 6 = 2 A, in phase with the larger current i1, giving 2 sin ωt A.

questions.questionText: The sum of v1 = 50 sin ωt V and v2 = 50 sin(ωt + 60°) V is:
If i1 = 8 sin ωt A and i2 = 6 sin(ωt − 90°) A, the difference i1 − i2 is:
questions.explanation: Reversing i2 gives 6 sin(ωt + 90°). Adding: R = √(8² + 6²) = 10 A at tan⁻¹(6/8) = +36.87°, so i1 − i2 = 10 sin(ωt + 36.87°) A.

questions.questionText: The phasor 3 + j4 expressed in polar form is:
The phasor 10∠−30° expressed in rectangular form is:
questions.explanation: a = 10 cos(−30°) = 8.66 and b = 10 sin(−30°) = −5, so the phasor is 8.66 − j5.

questions.questionText: Multiplying a phasor by the operator j:
options: Rotates it 90° clockwise without changing its magnitude
Rotates it 180° and doubles its magnitude
Rotates it 90° anticlockwise without changing its magnitude
Leaves its angle unchanged but reverses its sign
questions.explanation: j = 1∠90°, so multiplying by j adds 90° to the angle (anticlockwise) and leaves the length unchanged; j² = −1 is a 180° rotation.

questions.questionText: The product of the phasors (10∠30°) and (2∠−60°) is:
questions.explanation: In polar form magnitudes multiply and angles add: 10 × 2 = 20 and 30° + (−60°) = −30°, giving 20∠−30°.

questions.questionText: A voltage phasor 100∠0° V is divided by an impedance 20∠−36.87° Ω. The resulting current phasor is:
questions.explanation: Division divides magnitudes and subtracts angles: 100/20 = 5 and 0° − (−36.87°) = +36.87°, so I = 5∠36.87° A (a leading current).

questions.questionText: A 50 Hz sinusoidal current of peak value 15 A passes through zero, going positive, 2 ms after t = 0. Its equation is:
questions.explanation: ω = 2π × 50 = 314 rad/s. The wave starts 2 ms late, i.e. lags by 360° × 2/20 = 36°, so i = 15 sin(314t − 36°) A.

questions.questionText: In a circuit v = 100 sin(314t) V and i = 5 sin(314t − π/4) A. At the instant the voltage is at its positive peak, the current is:
questions.explanation: The voltage peaks at ωt = π/2, when i = 5 sin(π/2 − π/4) = 5 sin 45° = 3.54 A; the lagging current has not yet reached its own peak.

questions.questionText: The phasor of an alternating voltage completes 1500 revolutions in 30 s. The frequency of the voltage is:
questions.explanation: One revolution of the phasor is one cycle, so f = 1500/30 = 50 Hz.

questions.questionText: For a 50 Hz current i = 20 sin ωt A, the time taken for the current to rise from 10 A to 17.32 A for the first time is:
questions.explanation: 10 A occurs at θ = 30° and 17.32 A at θ = 60°. The 30° interval is (30/360) × 20 ms = 1.67 ms.

questions.questionText: Which statement about phase difference is correct?
options: It can be stated between a 50 Hz and a 60 Hz wave
It depends on the amplitudes of the two waves
It changes with time for two waves of equal frequency
It has a fixed value only between sinusoids of the same frequency
questions.explanation: For equal frequencies the angle between the waves stays constant; for different frequencies it keeps changing, and it is independent of amplitude.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements about phasors is NOT correct?
options: The length of a phasor may represent either the RMS or the peak value
Phasors are imagined to rotate anticlockwise at ω rad/s
Phasors of different frequencies can be added on the same phasor diagram
The vertical projection of a rotating phasor gives the instantaneous value
questions.explanation: A phasor diagram is a snapshot valid only for quantities of one frequency; waves of different frequencies cannot be combined as phasors. The other statements are true.

questions.questionText: A voltage v = Vm sin ωt is applied to a pure capacitor. The current is given by:
questions.explanation: In a capacitor i = C dv/dt = ωCVm cos ωt = Im sin(ωt + 90°), so the current leads the voltage by 90°.

questions.questionText: If the frequency of an alternating voltage is doubled, its time period:
questions.explanation: T = 1/f, so doubling f halves T.

questions.questionText: The standard frequency of the public electricity supply in Nepal is:
questions.explanation: Nepal's supply is 230 V single phase (400 V three phase) at 50 Hz, the same frequency as India; 60 Hz is used in countries such as the USA.

questions.questionText: AC circuit breakers interrupt current more easily than DC breakers of the same rating mainly because:
options: The AC current passes through zero twice in every cycle
AC has a lower peak value than DC
AC does not produce an arc
AC flows only on the surface of the contacts
questions.explanation: At each natural current zero the arc loses its energy and can be extinguished; a DC arc has no current zero and must be forced out.

questions.questionText: The main reason AC is preferred for long-distance power transmission is that:
options: AC flows with no I²R loss in the conductors
Its voltage can be stepped up and down efficiently with transformers
AC can be transmitted without insulators
questions.explanation: Transformers let the same power be sent at high voltage and low current, cutting I²R loss; AC lines still have resistance and reactance.

questions.questionText: The same power is transmitted over the same line, but the transmission voltage is raised 10 times. The I²R loss in the line:
options: Falls to 1/100 of its original value
Falls to 1/10 of its original value
questions.explanation: For the same power, I = P/V falls to 1/10, and the loss I²R falls to (1/10)² = 1/100 of its original value.

questions.questionText: Two voltage phasors 100∠0° V and 100∠120° V are added. The resultant is:
The phasor of a 50 Hz quantity rotates through what angle in 1 ms?
questions.explanation: The phasor turns 360° per cycle and makes 50 cycles per second, i.e. 18 000°/s, so in 1 ms it turns 18°.

questions.questionText: An alternating current of frequency 60 Hz has a maximum value of 12 A. Its value 1/360 s after it passes through zero going positive is:
The expression v = 30 sin ωt + 40 cos ωt V can be written as a single sinusoid:
questions.explanation: 40 cos ωt = 40 sin(ωt + 90°), in quadrature with 30 sin ωt. R = √(30² + 40²) = 50 V at tan⁻¹(40/30) = 53.13° leading.

questions.questionText: The voltage v = 325 sin(314t + 30°) V is represented by an RMS phasor of:
questions.explanation: The RMS phasor length is Vm/√2 = 325/1.414 = 229.8 V, and the angle is the phase angle +30°.

questions.questionText: The sinusoidal waveform is preferred for AC power systems mainly because:
options: It has the highest peak value for a given RMS value
Its average value over a full cycle is maximum
It contains many harmonics that help transmission
Its derivative and integral are sinusoids of the same frequency, so its shape is kept through R, L, C circuits and transformers
questions.explanation: Inductors and capacitors differentiate or integrate the waveform; only a sinusoid comes out with the same shape and frequency, merely scaled and shifted in phase.

questions.questionText: A 50 Hz voltage v = Vm sin ωt passes through zero going positive at t = 0. The current in the circuit reaches its first positive peak at t = 3 ms. The current:
questions.explanation: The voltage peaks at T/4 = 5 ms; the current peaks 2 ms earlier, so it leads by 360° × 2/20 = 36°.

subtopics.title: Generation of AC Voltage & Current
subtopics.subtitle: Faraday's law, e = Em sin ωt from a rotating coil, alternator parts and f = PN/120

concepts.text: Principle: Electromagnetic Induction

All AC generators work on Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction: whenever the magnetic flux linking a coil changes, an EMF is induced in the coil equal to the rate of change of flux linkage NΦ. Lenz's law supplies the sign: the induced EMF acts so as to oppose the change producing it, which is the minus sign in the equation. The flux linkage can be changed by moving a coil through a stationary field or by moving the field past a stationary coil; both arrangements are used in practice.

concepts.plainText: e = −N dΦ/dt

concepts.text: For a straight conductor of length l moving at velocity v through a uniform field B, the induced EMF is e = Blv when the motion is perpendicular to the field, and e = Blv sin θ when the velocity makes an angle θ with the field lines. The direction of the induced current is given by Fleming's right-hand rule: hold the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the right hand mutually perpendicular; with the thumb along the motion of the conductor and the forefinger along the field (N to S), the middle finger points along the induced current.

concepts.plainText: e = B l v sin θ

concepts.text: EMF of a Coil Rotating in a Uniform Field

Let a coil of N turns, each of area A, rotate at constant angular velocity ω in a uniform field B, starting with its plane perpendicular to the field, where the flux linked is maximum, Φm = BA. After time t the coil has turned through θ = ωt and the flux linked is Φ = BA cos ωt. Differentiating and applying Faraday's law gives e = NBAω sin ωt = Em sin ωt: the EMF is sinusoidal, with peak Em = NBAω = 2πfNBA. The EMF is zero where the flux linkage is maximum (coil plane perpendicular to B) and maximum where the flux linkage is zero (coil plane parallel to B), because there the coil sides cut the field lines fastest.

concepts.plainText: Φ = B A cos(ωt)
e = −N dΦ/dt = N B A ω sin(ωt) = Em sin(ωt)

concepts.text: What follows from the derivation:
items: The generated voltage and the current it drives have the general AC form v(t) = Vm sin(ωt + φ) and i(t) = Im sin(ωt + φ).
Vm and Im are the peak values, ω = 2πf rad/s is the angular frequency and φ is the phase angle.
Em = NBAω is proportional to the turns, flux density, coil area and speed; raising the speed raises both Em and f.
EMF and flux linkage are 90° apart: e is zero when Φ is maximum and maximum when Φ is zero.
Instantaneous EMF e = Em sin θ, where θ is the angle turned from the position of maximum flux linkage.

concepts.text: Single-Loop Alternator
Main parts of an elementary alternator:
items: Field system: permanent magnets or DC-excited electromagnets (N and S poles) that set up a uniform magnetic field.
Armature: the coil or loop in which the EMF is induced, mounted on a shaft driven by a prime mover (turbine or engine).
Slip rings: two continuous metal rings fixed to the shaft, each permanently connected to one end of the coil.
Brushes: stationary carbon blocks pressing on the slip rings, carrying the alternating current to the external load.
Because each coil end stays on its own ring, the load current reverses with the coil EMF, so the output is alternating.

concepts.text: In a 2-pole machine one complete revolution of the coil produces exactly one cycle of EMF: the load current flows one way while a coil side passes the N pole and the other way while it passes the S pole. In a machine with P poles each coil side passes P/2 pairs of poles per revolution, giving P/2 cycles, so the frequency is f = PN/120 with N the speed in revolutions per minute. Practical alternators are built inside out: the DC-excited field rotates and the armature winding is stationary, so the high-voltage, high-current output needs no sliding contacts and only the small field current passes through slip rings.

concepts.plainText: f = P N / 120  (P = number of poles, N in rpm)

rows: Very high (up to tens of kV)

concepts.text: Worked example: a 2-pole alternator is driven at 3000 rpm; its coil has 100 turns, each of area 0.02 m², in a uniform field of 0.5 T. Frequency f = PN/120 = 2 × 3000/120 = 50 Hz, so ω = 2π × 50 = 314 rad/s (equal to the mechanical speed 3000 × 2π/60 = 314 rad/s, as expected for 2 poles). Peak EMF Em = NBAω = 100 × 0.5 × 0.02 × 314 = 314 V and the RMS output is 314/√2 = 222 V. When the coil has turned 30° from the position of maximum flux linkage, e = 314 sin 30° = 157 V.
Going Deeper: The Generated EMF

The rotating-coil result can also be obtained by the cutting-of-flux method. Let each coil side have active length l and move in a circle of radius b/2, where b is the coil breadth, so its peripheral speed is v = ωb/2. At angle θ from the position of maximum flux linkage, only the velocity component perpendicular to the field, v sin θ, cuts flux, so each side generates Blv sin θ. The two sides of a turn add, giving 2Blv sin θ = Blbω sin θ = BAω sin θ per turn, exactly the result of the flux-linkage method.

concepts.latex: e = 2NBlv\sin\theta = NBA\omega\sin\theta,\qquad v = \frac{\omega b}{2},\; A = lb
concepts.plainText: e = 2 N B l v sin θ = N B A ω sin θ, with v = ωb/2 and A = l b

concepts.text: Since BA is the maximum flux Φm linked by one turn, the peak EMF can be written Em = NΦmω = 2πfNΦm. Dividing by √2 gives the RMS value, E = 4.44 f N Φm, the same EMF equation later used for transformers. It shows directly that at a fixed frequency the generated voltage is set by the turns and the flux, which in a real alternator is controlled through the DC field current.

concepts.plainText: E(rms) = 2π f N Φm / √2 = 4.44 f N Φm

concepts.text: In a machine with P poles, a coil side passes a N–S pole pair, and so completes one electrical cycle (360 electrical degrees), each time the rotor turns 720/P mechanical degrees. Electrical angle is therefore P/2 times mechanical angle, and the electrical angular frequency is P/2 times the mechanical angular speed. Putting the mechanical speed as N rpm gives f = (P/2)(N/60) = PN/120.

concepts.plainText: θe = (P/2) θm,  ωe = (P/2) ωm

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: 4-pole alternator, 1500 rpm, coil of 120 turns, Φm = 8 mWb
Frequency:      f = PN/120 = 4 × 1500/120 = 50 Hz
Peak EMF:       Em = 2πfNΦm = 2π × 50 × 120 × 0.008 = 301.6 V
RMS EMF:        E = Em/√2 = 213.3 V   (4.44 × 50 × 120 × 0.008 = 213.1 V)
Rotor turns 30° mechanical from the maximum-flux position:
                θe = (4/2) × 30° = 60° electrical
                e = 301.6 sin 60° = 261.2 V

Worked example 2 (cutting-of-flux method): 2-pole field, B = 0.8 T
Coil: 50 turns, length l = 0.4 m, breadth b = 0.2 m, speed 1500 rpm
ω = 2π × 1500/60 = 157.08 rad/s, f = 2 × 1500/120 = 25 Hz
Side speed:     v = ω × b/2 = 157.08 × 0.1 = 15.71 m/s
Per side peak:  Blv = 0.8 × 0.4 × 15.71 = 5.03 V
Per turn:       2 × 5.03 = 10.05 V
Coil peak:      Em = 50 × 10.05 = 502.7 V
Check:          NBAω = 50 × 0.8 × 0.08 × 157.08 = 502.7 V
Common mistakes in generation problems:
items: Putting the speed in rpm straight into Em = NBAω; convert first with ω = 2πN/60.
Leaving the coil area in cm²; 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m².
Using only one coil side in the cutting method; both sides of a turn contribute Blv.
Confusing poles with pole pairs: f = PN/120 uses the number of poles P, while f = p × n uses pole pairs p and speed n in rev/s.
Measuring θ from the wrong position: e = Em sin θ holds with θ taken from the plane of maximum flux linkage, not from the plane parallel to the field.
Treating the peak value as the RMS value when the question asks for the voltmeter reading.

concepts.text: At constant field, EMF and frequency are both proportional to speed: running an alternator 20% slow lowers both f and E by 20%. For a fixed 50 Hz, slow water turbines need many poles (24 poles at 250 rpm), while steam turbines use 2 or 4 poles at 3000 or 1500 rpm.

formulas.plainText: e = B l v sin θ
e = N B A ω sin(ωt) = Em sin(ωt)
Em = N B A ω = 2π f N B A

notes.text: f = PN/120 is a staple MCQ: 2 poles at 3000 rpm, 4 poles at 1500 rpm, 6 poles at 1000 rpm and 8 poles at 750 rpm all give 50 Hz. Rearranged, the synchronous speed is N = 120f/P.

The induced EMF is maximum when the flux linkage is zero (coil plane parallel to the field) and zero when the flux linkage is maximum (coil plane perpendicular to the field). Many candidates state the reverse; EMF depends on the rate of change of flux, not on the flux itself.

Slip rings deliver the coil EMF unchanged, so the output is AC; a commutator reverses the connections every half cycle, so the output is unidirectional. The EMF generated in the rotating coil is sinusoidal in both machines — only the collecting device differs.

Fleming's right-hand rule is for generators (direction of induced current); the left-hand rule is for motors (direction of force). In both, thumb = motion, forefinger = field, middle finger = current.

formulas.title: Faraday's law of induction
formulas.description: Induced EMF e in a coil of N turns equals the rate of change of the flux Φ (weber) linking it; the minus sign is Lenz's law.

formulas.title: Motional EMF in a conductor
formulas.plainText: e = B l v sin θ
formulas.description: EMF in a conductor of length l moving at velocity v through flux density B when the velocity makes angle θ with the field; e = Blv for perpendicular motion.

formulas.title: EMF of a rotating coil
formulas.plainText: e = N B A ω sin(ωt) = Em sin(ωt)
formulas.description: Instantaneous EMF of an N-turn coil of area A rotating at ω rad/s in a uniform field B, with time measured from the position of maximum flux linkage.

formulas.title: Peak generated EMF
formulas.plainText: Em = N B A ω = 2π f N B A
formulas.description: Peak value of the sinusoidal EMF from turns N, flux density B, coil area A and frequency f; divide by √2 for the RMS value.

formulas.title: Frequency of an alternator
formulas.description: Generated frequency in Hz from the number of poles P and the speed N in rpm; use N = 120f/P to find the speed needed for a given frequency.

flashcards.front: State Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction.
flashcards.back: The EMF induced in a coil equals the rate of change of flux linkage, e = −N dΦ/dt; the minus sign (Lenz's law) shows that the EMF opposes the change.

flashcards.front: At which position of a rotating coil is the generated EMF maximum?
flashcards.back: When the coil plane is parallel to the field: the flux linkage is then zero but changing fastest, so e = Em. With the plane perpendicular to the field (maximum flux) the EMF is zero.

flashcards.front: At what speed must a 4-pole alternator run to generate 50 Hz?
How does an alternator differ from a DC generator?
flashcards.back: Both induce a sinusoidal EMF in the armature coil; the alternator brings it out unchanged through slip rings (AC), while the DC generator uses a commutator to reverse the connections every half cycle, giving a unidirectional output.

questions.questionText: At what speed must a 6-pole alternator be driven to generate a 50 Hz supply?
A coil rotating at constant speed in a uniform magnetic field has maximum induced EMF when the plane of the coil is:
options: Perpendicular to the field, where the flux linkage is maximum
Parallel to the field, where the flux linkage is zero
questions.explanation: The EMF is −N dΦ/dt. The flux linkage BA cos ωt changes fastest when it passes through zero, i.e. when the coil plane is parallel to the field, so the EMF is maximum there.

questions.questionText: A coil of 50 turns, each of area 0.04 m², rotates at 3000 rpm in a uniform field of 0.2 T. The peak EMF generated is approximately:
In a simple single-loop alternator, the alternating EMF is brought out to the external circuit through:
questions.explanation: Each end of the rotating coil is fixed to its own continuous slip ring on which a stationary brush rests, so the output is delivered unchanged as AC; a commutator would make it unidirectional.

questions.questionText: A 4-pole alternator runs at 1800 rpm. The frequency of the generated EMF is:
The speed at which a 12-pole alternator must run to generate 50 Hz is:
An alternator driven at 375 rpm generates 50 Hz. The number of poles is:
According to Faraday's law, the EMF induced in a coil is proportional to:
options: The total flux linking the coil
The square of the current in the coil
The rate of change of flux linkage with the coil
questions.explanation: e = −N dΦ/dt: the EMF depends on how fast the flux linkage changes, not on the flux itself.

questions.questionText: Lenz's law is concerned with:
options: The magnitude of the induced EMF
The direction of the induced EMF or current
The force on a current-carrying conductor
questions.explanation: Lenz's law states that the induced EMF opposes the change of flux producing it, fixing its direction; this is the minus sign in Faraday's law.

questions.questionText: In Fleming's right-hand rule for a generator, the middle finger points in the direction of the:
questions.explanation: Thumb gives the motion, forefinger the field (N to S) and middle finger the induced current.

questions.questionText: A straight conductor moves parallel to the lines of a uniform magnetic field. The EMF induced in it is:
questions.explanation: e = Blv sin θ and θ = 0° for motion along the field, so no flux is cut and e = 0.

questions.questionText: A conductor 0.5 m long moves at 10 m/s at right angles to a uniform field of 0.6 T. The induced EMF is:
A conductor 0.4 m long moves at 20 m/s in a uniform field of 1.0 T, its velocity making an angle of 30° with the field lines. The induced EMF is:
questions.explanation: e = Blv sin θ = 1.0 × 0.4 × 20 × sin 30° = 8 × 0.5 = 4 V. Using cos 30° would give 6.93 V.

questions.questionText: In an alternator, the prime mover supplies:
options: Electrical energy to the load directly
Mechanical energy to rotate the rotor
questions.explanation: The prime mover (turbine or engine) provides the mechanical input that the alternator converts into electrical energy; the field is excited separately with DC.

questions.questionText: In most practical large alternators:
options: The armature rotates and the field is stationary
Both field and armature are stationary and the air gap rotates
The field system rotates and the armature winding is stationary
questions.explanation: Large alternators are of the rotating-field type, so the high-voltage armature output is taken from the stator without sliding contacts.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of the stationary-armature, rotating-field construction of alternators?
options: Only the low-voltage DC field current passes through slip rings
The stationary armature winding is easier to insulate for high voltage
The rotor carrying only the field winding is lighter, suiting high speeds
The armature current can be collected through a commutator
questions.explanation: An alternator uses no commutator at all; the armature output is taken from fixed stator terminals. The other three are genuine advantages.

questions.questionText: The field winding of an alternator is supplied with:
questions.explanation: The field poles must have a steady polarity, so they are excited with DC from an exciter or a rectifier, fed in through slip rings.

questions.questionText: An electrical generator converts:
questions.explanation: A generator is driven by a prime mover and delivers electrical output by electromagnetic induction; the reverse conversion is done by a motor.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the EMF in the armature coil of a DC generator is correct?
options: It is alternating; the commutator makes the output at the brushes unidirectional
It is unidirectional because the field is DC
It is unidirectional because the armature rotates in one direction
It is zero until the commutator connects the load
questions.explanation: Every rotating coil in a field generates an alternating EMF; the commutator reverses the coil connections every half cycle so the external output is DC.

questions.questionText: A coil of 100 turns rotating at 1000 rpm in a uniform field generates a peak EMF of 120 V. If the turns are increased to 150 and the speed to 1500 rpm, the field being unchanged, the new peak EMF is:
questions.explanation: Em = NBAω is proportional to both N and speed: Em = 120 × (150/100) × (1500/1000) = 120 × 1.5 × 1.5 = 270 V. Scaling by only one factor gives 180 V.

questions.questionText: The speed of a simple alternator is doubled and at the same time its field flux is halved. Compared with before:
options: The peak EMF and the frequency are both doubled
The peak EMF is unchanged and the frequency is doubled
The peak EMF is halved and the frequency is unchanged
The peak EMF and the frequency are both unchanged
questions.explanation: Em = NΦmω ∝ Φm × speed, so (1/2) × 2 = 1 leaves Em unchanged, while f = PN/120 depends only on speed and doubles.

questions.questionText: A coil generates a peak EMF of 250 V. The EMF when the coil has turned 60° from the position of maximum flux linkage is:
questions.explanation: e = Em sin θ = 250 × sin 60° = 216.5 V; 125 V would result from using cos 60°.

questions.questionText: A coil rotating in a uniform field has a peak EMF of 200 V. At the instant its plane makes an angle of 30° with the field lines, the EMF is:
questions.explanation: A plane parallel to the field is the maximum-EMF position, so 30° from it is θ = 90° − 30° = 60° from the maximum-flux position: e = 200 sin 60° = 173.2 V.

questions.questionText: A coil of 300 turns links a maximum flux of 5 mWb varying sinusoidally at 50 Hz. The RMS value of the induced EMF is:
questions.explanation: E = 4.44 f N Φm = 4.44 × 50 × 300 × 0.005 = 333 V; 471 V is the peak value 2πfNΦm.

questions.questionText: The rotor of a 4-pole alternator makes 25 revolutions per second. The frequency of the generated EMF is:
questions.explanation: With p = 2 pole pairs, f = p × n = 2 × 25 = 50 Hz (equivalently PN/120 = 4 × 1500/120).

questions.questionText: In an 8-pole machine, a mechanical rotation of 45° corresponds to an electrical angle of:
In a 6-pole alternator, one cycle of EMF is generated for every mechanical rotation of:
questions.explanation: One cycle = 360 electrical degrees = 360°/(P/2) = 360°/3 = 120° mechanical.

questions.questionText: The flux linking a coil of 400 turns changes uniformly from 2 mWb to 7 mWb in 0.1 s. The average EMF induced is:
questions.explanation: e = N ΔΦ/Δt = 400 × (7 − 2) × 10⁻³/0.1 = 20 V. Using the sum 9 mWb instead of the change gives 36 V.

questions.questionText: A coil of 100 turns in a 2-pole field links a maximum flux of 10 mWb and rotates at 3000 rpm. The average EMF over a half revolution, from +Φm to −Φm, is:
questions.explanation: In half a revolution the flux linkage changes by 2NΦm in T/2 = 10 ms: E(avg) = 2 × 100 × 0.01/0.01 = 200 V, i.e. 4fNΦm. The peak value would be 314 V.

questions.questionText: A 100-turn coil of area 0.02 m² rotates in a uniform field of 0.5 T. The speed needed for a peak EMF of 157 V is approximately:
A rectangular coil of 40 turns, 0.3 m long and 0.2 m wide, rotates at 3000 rpm in a uniform field of 0.5 T. Its peak EMF is approximately:
questions.explanation: A = 0.3 × 0.2 = 0.06 m² and ω = 2π × 3000/60 = 314.16 rad/s, so Em = NBAω = 40 × 0.5 × 0.06 × 314.16 = 377 V. Counting only one coil side gives 188.5 V.

questions.questionText: A 4-pole alternator running at 1500 rpm generates a peak EMF of 325 V. Taking t = 0 at zero EMF, its instantaneous EMF is:
questions.explanation: f = 4 × 1500/120 = 50 Hz, so the electrical ω = 2π × 50 = 314 rad/s. 157 rad/s is the mechanical speed, not the electrical angular frequency.

questions.questionText: A 2-pole alternator runs at 3000 rpm and its coil has a peak EMF of 300 V. The EMF 3.33 ms after the coil passes the position of maximum flux linkage is approximately:
If the slip rings of an elementary single-loop alternator are replaced by a split-ring commutator, the voltage across the load becomes:
questions.explanation: The commutator reverses the coil connections every half revolution, so both half cycles appear with the same polarity at the load: a pulsating unidirectional voltage.

questions.questionText: For a coil rotating in a magnetic field to generate a purely sinusoidal EMF, which condition is NOT required?
options: The magnetic field must be uniform
The coil must have a large number of turns
The angular velocity must be constant
The field strength must not vary with time
questions.explanation: The number of turns only scales the amplitude; the sine shape comes from a uniform, steady (time-invariant) field and rotation at constant angular velocity.

questions.questionText: For a coil rotating in a uniform field with Φ = Φm cos ωt, the induced EMF:
options: Is in phase with the flux
Is 180° out of phase with the flux
questions.explanation: e = −N dΦ/dt = NΦmω sin ωt = Em cos(ωt − 90°), so the EMF reaches its peak a quarter cycle after the flux: it lags by 90°.

questions.questionText: If the number of turns of the rotating coil of a simple alternator is doubled, speed and field remaining the same:
options: The peak EMF and the frequency both double
The peak EMF doubles and the frequency is unchanged
The frequency doubles and the peak EMF is unchanged
questions.explanation: Em = NBAω is proportional to N, while the frequency depends only on the speed and the number of poles.

questions.questionText: The frequency of the EMF generated by an alternator depends on:
options: The number of poles and the rotor speed only
The number of poles, the rotor speed and the field current
The rotor speed and the number of armature turns
The flux density and the coil area
questions.explanation: f = PN/120 contains only the pole number and speed; field current, turns, flux density and area change the magnitude of the EMF, not its frequency.

questions.questionText: Alternators driven by water turbines in hydro plants usually have a large number of poles because:
options: Water turbines run at low speed, so many poles are needed to give 50 Hz
More poles increase the terminal voltage without limit
More poles reduce the frequency to 25 Hz
Hydro alternators have no field winding
questions.explanation: From P = 120f/N, a low turbine speed requires many poles for 50 Hz, e.g. 24 poles at 250 rpm.

questions.questionText: An alternator generates 60 Hz when driven at 1200 rpm. The speed at which the same machine must run to generate 50 Hz is:
questions.explanation: P = 120 × 60/1200 = 6 poles; for 50 Hz, N = 120 × 50/6 = 1000 rpm. Running at 1440 rpm would give 72 Hz.

questions.questionText: The N-pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards the face of a closed coil. The face of the coil nearest the magnet becomes:
questions.explanation: By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the approaching N-pole, so the near face becomes a north pole and repels the magnet.

questions.questionText: The EMF induced in the armature winding of an alternator is best described as:
questions.explanation: The EMF results from relative motion between the conductors and the field, which is dynamically (motionally) induced EMF, whichever of the two actually moves.

questions.questionText: A magnetic flux density of 1 tesla is equal to:
questions.explanation: Flux density B is flux per unit area, so 1 T = 1 weber per square metre.

questions.questionText: A coil of 80 turns, each of area 250 cm², rotates at ω = 314.16 rad/s in a uniform field of 0.3 T. The peak EMF is approximately:
questions.explanation: A = 250 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.025 m², so Em = NBAω = 80 × 0.3 × 0.025 × 314.16 = 188.5 V. Converting with 10⁻³ instead of 10⁻⁴ gives the tenfold error 1885 V.

questions.questionText: A 250-turn coil links a maximum flux of 4 mWb in a 50 Hz alternator. The EMF 1/600 s after the coil passes the position of maximum flux linkage is approximately:
In a 60 Hz alternator, the time between the instant of maximum flux linkage in a coil and the next instant of maximum EMF in it is:
questions.explanation: Flux linkage and EMF are 90° apart, i.e. a quarter period: T/4 = (1/60)/4 = 4.17 ms.

questions.questionText: An alternator with constant field excitation produces 240 V at 50 Hz. If its speed is reduced until the frequency is 40 Hz, the EMF becomes:
questions.explanation: With constant flux, E ∝ speed ∝ f, so E = 240 × 40/50 = 192 V.

questions.questionText: A vehicle's steel axle 1.5 m long moves horizontally at 72 km/h where the vertical component of the earth's field is 40 µT. The EMF between the ends of the axle is:
questions.explanation: v = 72/3.6 = 20 m/s, so e = Blv = 40 × 10⁻⁶ × 1.5 × 20 = 1.2 × 10⁻³ V = 1.2 mV. Using 72 without converting gives 4.32 mV.

questions.questionText: Which statement about an elementary 2-pole single-loop alternator is NOT correct?
options: One revolution of the coil produces two cycles of EMF
Each slip ring stays connected to the same end of the coil
The EMF reverses every half revolution
The output frequency in Hz equals the number of revolutions per second
questions.explanation: In a 2-pole machine one revolution gives exactly one cycle (P/2 = 1), so f equals rev/s; two cycles per revolution would need 4 poles.

questions.questionText: The armature core of an alternator is built from thin laminations of silicon steel in order to:
options: Increase the resistance of the armature winding
Allow AC to be converted to DC
questions.explanation: The core carries alternating flux; thin insulated laminations limit eddy currents and silicon steel has a narrow hysteresis loop.

subtopics.title: Peak, Average, and RMS Values
subtopics.subtitle: Vrms = 0.707 Vm, Vavg = 0.637 Vm, form factor 1.11 and peak factor 1.414

concepts.text: Peak, Average, and RMS Values

An alternating quantity changes continuously, so a single number is needed to state how large it is. Four are used: the peak (maximum) value, the peak-to-peak value, the average (mean) value and the root-mean-square (RMS) or effective value. Unless a question says otherwise, AC voltages and currents are always quoted as RMS values, and the sinusoidal factors below apply only to sine waves.
Peak value (Vm): the maximum value of the waveform amplitude, measured from zero; for a symmetrical wave the peak-to-peak value is 2Vm.
items: Vm = 1.414 × Vrms (sine wave)
Form factor = Vrms / Vavg = 1.11
Peak factor = Vm / Vrms = 1.414
Peak-to-peak value Vp-p = 2 Vm

concepts.text: Average Value

The average value is the arithmetic mean of the instantaneous values over a stated interval. For a symmetrical wave such as a sinusoid the positive and negative half cycles cancel, so the average over a full cycle is zero; the average is therefore taken over one half cycle. Integrating Vm sin θ from 0 to π and dividing by π gives Vavg = 2Vm/π = 0.637 Vm. The average value is what a rectifier delivers as DC and what a moving-coil instrument responds to.

concepts.plainText: Vavg = (1/π) ∫₀^π Vm sin θ dθ = 2Vm/π = 0.637 Vm

concepts.text: RMS (Effective) Value

The RMS value of an alternating current is the steady direct current that produces the same heat in the same resistance in the same time; it is also called the effective or virtual value. Because heating power is proportional to the square of the current, the RMS value is found by squaring the instantaneous values, taking the mean of the squares over a full cycle and then the square root. For i = Im sin θ the mean of sin²θ over a cycle is 1/2, giving Irms = Im/√2 = 0.707 Im. RMS values are used in every power calculation, P = Vrms Irms cos φ = Irms² R, and are what AC meters indicate.

concepts.plainText: Vrms = 0.707 Vm; Vavg = 0.637 Vm
Irms = √[(1/2π) ∫₀^2π Im² sin²θ dθ] = Im/√2

concepts.text: Form Factor and Peak Factor

Form factor = RMS value / average value describes the shape of the wave: 1.11 for a sine, 1.0 for a square wave and 1.155 for a triangular wave. Average-reading (rectifier) meters are scaled by 1.11 so that they read RMS for sinusoids. Peak (crest) factor = peak value / RMS value shows how far the peaks rise above the effective value: 1.414 for a sine, 1.0 for a square wave and 1.732 for a triangular wave; it matters for insulation stress and for the voltage ratings of capacitors and semiconductors.
Why Meters Read RMS

Moving-iron, electrodynamometer and thermal instruments respond to the square of the current, so they indicate true RMS for any waveform. Rectifier-type moving-coil meters and most low-cost digital multimeters measure the average of the rectified wave and multiply it by the sine form factor 1.11, so they read correctly only for sinusoidal quantities. Because heating, power and equipment ratings all depend on the RMS value, nameplate figures and the 230 V mains are always RMS.

Worked examples:
1. Nepal mains, 230 V RMS: Vm = 230 × √2 = 325 V, Vp-p = 650 V, and Vavg (half cycle) = 0.637 × 325 = 207 V, or 230/1.11 = 207 V.
2. A sinusoidal current of peak 10 A flows in 5 Ω: Irms = 7.07 A, Iavg = 6.37 A, and the power is Irms² R = 7.07² × 5 = 250 W, not Im² R = 500 W.
3. A square wave of amplitude 100 V: Vrms = Vavg = 100 V, so its form factor and peak factor are both 1.
Going Deeper: RMS, Average and Waveform Factors

The factor 1/√2 comes from the identity sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2. Over one full cycle the cos 2θ term averages to zero, so the mean of sin²θ is exactly 1/2 and the mean of v² is Vm²/2; its square root is Vm/√2. The result is the same for a cosine or for a sine with any phase angle, and it does not depend on frequency. For the average, the area under one half cycle of Vm sin θ is 2Vm, and dividing by the base π gives 2Vm/π.

concepts.plainText: Mean of sin²θ = (1/2π) ∫₀^2π sin²θ dθ = 1/2

concepts.text: When a waveform is the sum of a DC component and sinusoids of different frequencies, every cross-product term averages to zero over a common period. The heating effects therefore add: the square of the total RMS value equals the sum of the squares of the individual RMS values. RMS values of components at different frequencies never add arithmetically, and the full-cycle average of such a wave equals its DC component alone.

concepts.plainText: Vrms = √(V0² + V1rms² + V2rms² + …), V0 = DC component

concepts.text:
Example 1: v = 10 + 20 sin ωt V applied to a 10 Ω resistor
DC part: V0 = 10 V
AC part: RMS = 20/√2 = 14.14 V
Vrms = √(10² + 14.14²) = √(100 + 200) = 17.32 V
Full-cycle average = V0 = 10 V
P = Vrms²/R = 300/10 = 30 W
Check: DC alone gives 10 W, AC alone gives 20 W, total 30 W

Example 2: half-wave rectified sine, peak Vm = 100 V
Average: one hump has area 2Vm, the period is 2π
  Vavg = 2Vm/(2π) = Vm/π = 31.8 V
RMS: v² exists for only half the period
  mean of v² = (1/2)(Vm²/2) = Vm²/4, so Vrms = Vm/2 = 50 V
Form factor = 50/31.8 = 1.57
Peak factor = 100/50 = 2.0

concepts.plainText: Rectangular pulse train 0 to Vm with duty cycle D: Vavg = D Vm, Vrms = √D Vm

concepts.text:
Example 3: pulse train switching 0 V to 12 V, duty cycle D = 0.25
Vavg = D × Vm = 0.25 × 12 = 3 V
Vrms = √D × Vm = 0.5 × 12 = 6 V
Form factor = 6/3 = 2.0, peak factor = 12/6 = 2.0
A sine-calibrated average-reading meter would show 1.11 × 3 = 3.33 V
Common mistakes to avoid:
items: Using 0.707 and 0.637 for square, triangular, pulse or rectified waves; these factors belong to the pure sine only.
Adding RMS values of components of different frequencies arithmetically instead of as a root-sum-of-squares.
Using the peak value in P = I²R, which doubles the power of a sine wave.
Taking the full-cycle average of a half-wave rectified sine as 0.637 Vm; it is Vm/π = 0.318 Vm.
Forgetting that the peak-to-peak value is twice the peak value, i.e. 2√2 times the RMS value for a sine.

concepts.text: Sanity check: the RMS value is never smaller than the average of the magnitude, and the peak is never smaller than the RMS value, so form factor and peak factor are always at least 1. They equal 1 only when the magnitude is constant, as for DC or a square wave. A computed factor below 1 means a slip in the working.

notes.text: Mains '230 V' is an RMS value. Its peak is 230 × 1.414 ≈ 325 V — a favourite one-mark question.
For non-sinusoidal waveforms the 0.707/0.637 factors do NOT apply; compute RMS and average from their definitions (for a square wave RMS = average = Vm).

The average of any symmetrical AC wave over a full cycle is zero. When a question asks for 'the average value' of a sinusoid it means the half-cycle average 0.637 Vm unless it explicitly says 'over a complete cycle'.
Power always uses RMS values: P = Irms² R = Vrms² / R. Substituting the peak value doubles the answer for a sine wave, because Im² = 2 Irms².

formulas.title: RMS value of a sinusoid
formulas.description: Effective (heating) value of a sine wave from its peak Vm; use RMS in all power calculations and for meter readings.

formulas.title: Average value of a sinusoid
formulas.description: Mean of a sine wave over one half cycle (the full-cycle mean is zero); used for rectifier output and moving-coil meter deflection.

formulas.title: Form factor
formulas.description: Ratio of RMS to average value, 1.11 for a sine wave; it converts an average-reading meter scale to RMS.

formulas.title: Peak (crest) factor
formulas.description: Ratio of peak to RMS value, √2 for a sine wave; gives the peak voltage that insulation and capacitors must withstand.

formulas.title: General RMS definition
formulas.description: Root of the mean of the squared instantaneous values over one period T; use it for any waveform when the sine-wave factors do not apply.

flashcards.front: Define the RMS value of an alternating current.
flashcards.back: The steady DC current that produces the same heat in the same resistor in the same time; for a sine wave Irms = Im/√2 = 0.707 Im.

flashcards.front: What are the peak and peak-to-peak values of the 230 V mains?
flashcards.back: Vm = 230 × √2 ≈ 325 V and Vp-p ≈ 650 V; the quoted 230 V is the RMS value.

flashcards.front: What are the form factor and peak factor of a square wave?
flashcards.back: Both equal 1.0, because for a square wave the RMS, average and peak values are all the same.

flashcards.front: Why is the average value of a sine wave taken over half a cycle?
flashcards.back: Over a full cycle the positive and negative halves cancel to zero; the half-cycle average 2Vm/π = 0.637 Vm is the useful figure, e.g. for rectifier output.

questions.questionText: A sinusoidal current has an RMS value of 5 A. Its peak value is:
The RMS value of an alternating current is defined as the:
options: Arithmetic mean of all instantaneous values over one half cycle
Steady direct current that produces the same heat in a given resistance in the same time
Maximum instantaneous value reached during a cycle
Average of the positive and negative peak values
questions.explanation: The RMS (effective) value is defined by heating equivalence with DC; the half-cycle mean is the average value and the maximum is the peak value.

questions.questionText: A sinusoidal voltage has a peak value of 50 V. Its average value taken over one half cycle is:
The voltage v = 311 sin 314t V is applied to a circuit. Its RMS value and frequency are:
Which instrument indicates the true RMS value of a current regardless of its waveform?
questions.explanation: The moving-iron deflecting torque is proportional to i², so it responds to the mean square; PMMC responds to the average and rectifier meters to the rectified average scaled by 1.11.

questions.questionText: The peak-to-peak value of a 12 V (RMS) sinusoidal voltage is:
A permanent-magnet moving-coil (PMMC) voltmeter without a rectifier is connected across a pure 50 Hz sinusoidal supply of 230 V. It reads:
questions.explanation: A PMMC meter responds to the average value, and the average of a symmetrical sine wave over a full cycle is zero, so the pointer stays at zero.

questions.questionText: An average-responding (rectifier-type) voltmeter whose scale is calibrated to read RMS for sine waves is connected to a symmetrical square wave of amplitude ±100 V. The meter reads:
questions.explanation: The rectified average of the square wave is 100 V; the meter multiplies by the sine form factor 1.11 and shows 111 V, although the true RMS is 100 V.

questions.questionText: An average-responding voltmeter calibrated in RMS for sine waves is used on a symmetrical triangular wave of peak 100 V. The error of its reading relative to the true RMS value is:
questions.explanation: Rectified average = 0.5 × 100 = 50 V, so the meter shows 1.11 × 50 = 55.5 V; true RMS = 100/√3 = 57.7 V; error = (55.5 − 57.7)/57.7 = −3.9 %.

questions.questionText: Crest factor is another name for:
questions.explanation: Crest factor and peak factor both mean peak value divided by RMS value; form factor is RMS divided by average.

questions.questionText: A half-wave rectified sine wave has a peak value of 20 V. Its average value over one complete cycle is:
questions.explanation: For half-wave rectification Vavg = Vm/π = 20/3.1416 = 6.37 V; 12.7 V (2Vm/π) would be the full-wave value.

questions.questionText: The RMS value of a half-wave rectified sine wave of peak value 30 V is:
questions.explanation: Only half of each cycle contributes to the mean square, so Vrms = Vm/2 = 30/2 = 15.0 V.

questions.questionText: For which waveform is the form factor equal to exactly 1?
questions.explanation: A square wave has constant magnitude, so its RMS and average values are both Vm and FF = 1; the others give 1.11, 1.155 and 1.57.

questions.questionText: A full-wave rectified sine wave has a peak value of 100 V. Its average (DC) value is:
questions.explanation: Each half cycle is a positive hump, so Vavg = 2Vm/π = 0.637 × 100 = 63.7 V over the whole cycle.

questions.questionText: Among the following waveforms of equal peak value, which has the highest peak factor?
questions.explanation: Peak factors: triangular 1.732, sine 1.414, full-wave rectified sine 1.414, square 1.0.

questions.questionText: A symmetrical square wave alternating between +10 V and −10 V is applied to a 5 Ω resistor. The average power dissipated is:
questions.explanation: For a square wave Vrms = Vm = 10 V, so P = Vrms²/R = 100/5 = 20 W; the sine factor 0.707 does not apply.

questions.questionText: A symmetrical triangular voltage wave has a peak value of 30 V. Its RMS value is:
questions.explanation: For a triangular wave Vrms = Vm/√3 = 30/1.732 = 17.3 V; 21.2 V would wrongly use the sine factor.

questions.questionText: Which statement about RMS, form factor and peak factor is NOT correct?
options: An average-responding meter calibrated for sine waves reads the true RMS value of a square wave
The form factor of a pure sine wave is 1.11
The RMS value of a steady DC voltage equals the DC voltage itself
The peak factor of a symmetrical square wave is 1
questions.explanation: An average-responding meter multiplies the rectified average by 1.11, so on a square wave it reads 11 % high; the other three statements are true.

questions.questionText: A current i = 3 + 4√2 sin ωt A flows through a 10 Ω resistor. The average power dissipated is:
questions.explanation: DC part 3 A, AC part RMS = 4 A; Irms² = 3² + 4² = 25 A², so P = 25 × 10 = 250 W.

questions.questionText: Alternating voltages and currents are normally specified by their RMS values mainly because:
options: RMS values are always larger than peak values
RMS values are zero over a complete cycle and simplify calculation
RMS values give the same heating and power as the equal DC value, so P = VI and P = I²R stay valid
RMS values do not depend on the waveform shape
questions.explanation: The RMS value is defined by equal heating, so power formulas used for DC hold directly; RMS is smaller than the peak and does depend on waveform shape.

questions.questionText: The current i = 10 sin ωt + 10 sin 3ωt A contains a fundamental and a third harmonic. Its RMS value is:
questions.explanation: Components of different frequency add as squares: Irms = √[(10/√2)² + (10/√2)²] = √(50 + 50) = 10.0 A.

questions.questionText: The exact value of the form factor of a pure sine wave is:
questions.explanation: FF = (Vm/√2)/(2Vm/π) = π/(2√2) = 1.11; π/2 = 1.57 is the half-wave rectified value.

questions.questionText: A sinusoidal current flowing through a 100 Ω resistor dissipates 200 W. The peak value of the current is:
If the peak value of a sinusoidal voltage applied to a fixed resistor is doubled, the power dissipated becomes:
questions.explanation: Vrms doubles with the peak, and P = Vrms²/R, so the power becomes 2² = 4 times.

questions.questionText: A 1 kW, 230 V (RMS) electric heater is operated on a sinusoidal supply. The peak value of the heater current is:
The peak value of a sinusoidal voltage is kept constant while its frequency is raised from 50 Hz to 60 Hz. Its RMS value:
questions.explanation: Vrms = Vm/√2 depends only on the amplitude and waveform shape, not on the frequency.

questions.questionText: An alternating voltage waveform has an RMS value of 50 V, an average value of 40 V and a peak value of 80 V. Its form factor and peak factor are:
questions.explanation: Form factor = RMS/average = 50/40 = 1.25; peak factor = peak/RMS = 80/50 = 1.6.

questions.questionText: The form factor of a half-wave rectified sine wave is:
questions.explanation: FF = Vrms/Vavg = (Vm/2)/(Vm/π) = π/2 = 1.57; 2.0 is its peak factor.

questions.questionText: A capacitor is connected directly across a 240 V (RMS), 50 Hz sinusoidal supply. The maximum instantaneous voltage the capacitor dielectric must withstand is:
questions.explanation: Vm = √2 × 240 = 339 V; the dielectric is stressed by the peak value, not the RMS value.

questions.questionText: The dielectric strength of insulation in an AC system must be chosen on the basis of the:
questions.explanation: Breakdown occurs when the instantaneous stress exceeds the dielectric strength, so the peak (maximum) voltage governs insulation design.

questions.questionText: A 50 Hz sinusoidal voltage of RMS value 100 V passes through zero going positive at t = 0. Its instantaneous value at t = 2.5 ms is:
In deriving the RMS value of a sine wave, the mean value of sin²θ over one complete cycle is:
questions.explanation: sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2 and cos 2θ averages to zero over a cycle, leaving 1/2; hence Vrms = Vm/√2.

questions.questionText: A rectangular pulse train switches between 0 V and 10 V with a duty cycle of 20 %. Its RMS value is:
questions.explanation: Vrms = √D × Vm = √0.2 × 10 = 4.47 V; the average would be D × Vm = 2 V.

questions.questionText: A true-RMS voltmeter and a sine-calibrated average-responding voltmeter both read exactly 10 V on the same AC signal. The signal is most likely:
questions.explanation: The average-responding meter is correct only when the form factor is 1.11, i.e. for a sine wave; it reads high on a square wave (FF = 1) and low on a triangle or a narrow pulse train (FF above 1.11).

questions.questionText: The output of a full-wave rectifier is a rectified sine of peak 12 V. A moving-coil DC voltmeter and a true-RMS voltmeter connected across it read respectively:
questions.explanation: The moving-coil meter reads the average 2Vm/π = 0.637 × 12 = 7.64 V; the RMS of a full-wave rectified sine equals Vm/√2 = 8.49 V.

questions.questionText: When a sine wave is full-wave rectified, its RMS value:
options: Remains the same as that of the original sine
questions.explanation: Rectification only reverses the negative half cycles; v² is unchanged at every instant, so the RMS value stays Vm/√2.

questions.questionText: A half-wave rectified sinusoidal current of peak 10 A flows through a 20 Ω resistor. The average power dissipated is:
questions.explanation: Irms of a half-wave rectified sine = Im/2 = 5 A; P = Irms² R = 25 × 20 = 500 W.

questions.questionText: Compared with a full-wave rectified sine wave of the same peak value, a half-wave rectified sine wave has:
options: Half the average value and half the RMS value
Half the average value and 1/√2 times the RMS value
The same average value and half the RMS value
Half the average value and the same RMS value
questions.explanation: Averages: Vm/π versus 2Vm/π, a ratio of 1/2; RMS: Vm/2 versus Vm/√2, a ratio of 1/√2 because the mean square is halved.

questions.questionText: The voltage v = 30√2 sin ωt + 40√2 sin 2ωt V is applied to a true-RMS voltmeter. The meter reads:
questions.explanation: Component RMS values are 30 V and 40 V at different frequencies, so Vrms = √(30² + 40²) = 50 V, not 30 + 40 = 70 V.

questions.questionText: A sawtooth voltage rises linearly from 0 to 9 V and then drops instantly back to zero, repeating every period. Its RMS value is:
questions.explanation: For a linear ramp from 0 to Vm, mean of v² = Vm²/3, so Vrms = Vm/√3 = 9/1.732 = 5.20 V; 4.50 V is the average.

questions.questionText: The RMS value of an alternating quantity is also called its:
questions.explanation: RMS, effective and virtual value are synonyms; mean is the average and crest is the peak.

questions.questionText: For the voltage v = 5 + 10 sin ωt V, the average value over one complete cycle and the RMS value are respectively:
questions.explanation: Full-cycle average = DC part = 5 V; Vrms = √(5² + (10/√2)²) = √(25 + 50) = 8.66 V.

questions.questionText: A sinusoidal voltage of peak 10 V is applied across a 10 Ω resistor for one minute. The heat energy produced is:
questions.explanation: Vrms = 7.07 V, P = Vrms²/R = 50/10 = 5 W; energy = 5 × 60 = 300 J.

subtopics.title: Three Phase System
subtopics.subtitle: Three EMFs 120° apart, star and delta relations, P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ

concepts.text: Three Phase System

A three-phase system has three sinusoidal EMFs of equal magnitude and frequency, displaced from one another by 120° (one third of a cycle). They are generated by three identical windings spaced 120° apart on the stator of an alternator and are labelled R, Y, B (red, yellow, blue) or L1, L2, L3. Phase sequence is the order in which the three voltages reach their positive maxima; RYB is the normal (positive) sequence, and interchanging any two lines reverses it and reverses the rotation of three-phase motors. In a balanced system the three voltages add to zero at every instant.

concepts.plainText: vR = Vm sin ωt, vY = Vm sin(ωt − 120°), vB = Vm sin(ωt − 240°) = Vm sin(ωt + 120°)

concepts.text: STAR (Y) CONNECTION:
items: Line voltage V_L = √3 × phase voltage V_ph; each line voltage leads its phase voltage by 30°.
Line current I_L = phase current I_ph.
Has a neutral wire: the common point of the three windings, giving a 3-phase 4-wire supply.
Two voltages are available: V_ph between any line and neutral, V_L between any two lines.

concepts.text: In a star connection one end of each winding (or load impedance) is joined to a common neutral point N and the other ends go to the three lines. Each line is in series with its winding, so I_L = I_ph. The voltage between two lines is the phasor difference of two phase voltages 120° apart, which has magnitude 2 V_ph cos 30° = √3 V_ph. In a balanced star system the three line currents sum to zero, so the neutral carries no current and a 3-wire supply is possible; the neutral is needed when single-phase loads make the system unbalanced.
DELTA (Δ) CONNECTION:
items: Line voltage V_L = phase voltage V_ph.
Line current I_L = √3 × phase current I_ph; each line current lags its phase current by 30°.
No neutral wire: only a 3-phase 3-wire supply is possible.
Used for motor windings, transformer windings and balanced three-phase loads.

concepts.text: In a delta connection the three windings are joined end to end in a closed loop and the lines are taken from the three junctions. Each winding is connected directly across two lines, so V_L = V_ph. Each line current is the phasor difference of the two phase currents meeting at that junction, 120° apart, hence I_L = √3 I_ph. Delta has no neutral and cannot supply single-phase loads at phase voltage, but the same impedance connected in delta draws three times the power it draws in star from the same lines.
Three Phase Power
THREE PHASE POWER (balanced load; φ is the angle between phase voltage and phase current):
items: Active power P = √3 × V_L × I_L × cos φ = 3 × V_ph × I_ph × cos φ, in watts (W).
Reactive power Q = √3 × V_L × I_L × sin φ = 3 × V_ph × I_ph × sin φ, in VAR.
Apparent power S = √3 × V_L × I_L = 3 × V_ph × I_ph = √(P² + Q²), in VA.
Power factor cos φ = P / S; the formulas are identical for star and delta connections.

concepts.plainText: P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ = 3 V_ph I_ph cos φ
Q = √3 V_L I_L sin φ;  S = √3 V_L I_L = √(P² + Q²)

concepts.text: A load is balanced when the three phase impedances are equal in magnitude and angle; the three currents are then equal and 120° apart, the neutral current is zero, and the total instantaneous power is constant at 3 V_ph I_ph cos φ instead of pulsating at twice the supply frequency as in a single-phase circuit. With an unbalanced load the three currents differ, the neutral (if present) carries their phasor sum, and the power in each phase must be calculated separately and added. Unequal loads on a 3-wire star system also shift the neutral point, giving unequal phase voltages.
Advantages of three phase over single phase:
items: Constant, non-pulsating power flow, so motors and generators run smoothly with less vibration.
Three-phase motors are self-starting (the windings produce a rotating magnetic field), simpler and smaller for the same output.
For the same power, voltage and line loss, three-phase 3-wire transmission needs only about 75 % of the conductor material of single-phase 2-wire.
Two voltages (400 V and 230 V) are available from one 4-wire supply, and rectified three-phase output has less ripple.

concepts.text: Power in a three-phase, three-wire circuit is measured by the two-wattmeter method: the current coil of each wattmeter is placed in one line and its pressure coil is connected between that line and the third line. The total power is P = W1 + W2 for any load, balanced or unbalanced. For a balanced load the readings also give the power factor from tan φ = √3 (W1 − W2)/(W1 + W2): the readings are equal at unity power factor, one reads zero at cos φ = 0.5, and below 0.5 one reading is negative and must be subtracted.

Worked example (Nepal supply): the three-phase distribution voltage is 400 V between lines, so the phase (line-to-neutral) voltage is 400/√3 = 231 V, the single-phase 230 V household supply. A balanced star load draws 20 A per line at power factor 0.8 lagging: S = √3 × 400 × 20 = 13.86 kVA, P = 13.86 × 0.8 = 11.08 kW and Q = 13.86 × 0.6 = 8.31 kVAR; each phase impedance is Z = 231/20 = 11.55 Ω. Reconnected in delta on the same 400 V lines, each impedance sees 400 V, so I_ph = 400/11.55 = 34.6 A, I_L = √3 × 34.6 = 60 A and P = √3 × 400 × 60 × 0.8 = 33.3 kW, three times the star value.
Going Deeper: Solving Three-Phase Circuits

Take V_R = V_ph∠0° and V_Y = V_ph∠−120°. The line voltage V_RY = V_R − V_Y is the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by V_R and −V_Y, which are 60° apart, so its length is 2 V_ph cos 30° = √3 V_ph and it sits 30° ahead of V_R. The same construction applied to the two phase currents meeting at a delta junction gives I_L = √3 I_ph, with the line current 30° behind the phase current.

A balanced circuit is solved on a per-phase basis: find one phase voltage, divide by one phase impedance, and multiply the phase power by three. A delta load may first be replaced by its equivalent star, Z_Y = Z_Δ/3, and solved with V_ph = V_L/√3; both routes give the same line current and total power. The load angle φ is the angle of the phase impedance Z = R + jX, so cos φ = R/|Z| and P = 3 I_ph² R.

concepts.plainText: W1 = V_L I_L cos(30° − φ), W2 = V_L I_L cos(30° + φ) (balanced load, lagging pf)

concepts.text: Adding the two readings gives W1 + W2 = √3 V_L I_L cos φ, the total active power. Subtracting gives W1 − W2 = V_L I_L sin φ, so the total reactive power of a balanced load is Q = √3 (W1 − W2), and dividing the two results gives the familiar tan φ = √3 (W1 − W2)/(W1 + W2). The table shows how the ratio of the readings changes with the load power factor.

rows: W2 reads zero, W1 gives total power
Reverse a coil of W2 and subtract its reading
Readings equal and opposite, total power zero

concepts.text:
Example 2: two-wattmeter method, balanced load, W1 = 5 kW, W2 = 2 kW
P = W1 + W2 = 7 kW
tan φ = √3 (W1 − W2)/(W1 + W2) = √3 × 3/7 = 0.742
φ = 36.6°, power factor = cos 36.6° = 0.803 lagging
Q = √3 (W1 − W2) = √3 × 3 = 5.20 kVAR
Check: P tan φ = 7 × 0.742 = 5.20 kVAR

Example 3: unbalanced 4-wire star, resistive loads, RYB sequence
I_R = 10∠0° A = 10 + j0
I_Y = 20∠−120° A = −10 − j17.32
I_B = 30∠+120° A = −15 + j25.98
I_N = I_R + I_Y + I_B = −15 + j8.66
|I_N| = √(15² + 8.66²) = √(225 + 75) = 17.32 A
Note: the arithmetic sum 60 A or the difference 20 A are both wrong
Special cases worth remembering (balanced resistive loads, fixed supply):
items: Star load on a 3-wire supply with one phase open: the other two phases are in series across V_L and the total power falls to one half.
Delta load with one phase open: the remaining two phases still see V_L, so the total power falls to two thirds.
Star-delta starter: each winding gets V_L/√3 at starting, so line current and starting torque both fall to one third of their direct-on-line delta values.
An unbalanced 3-phase 4-wire load needs three wattmeters; two are enough for any 3-wire load (Blondel's theorem: one fewer than the number of wires).

concepts.text: Common slips: dividing the line voltage by a star phase impedance (use V_ph = V_L/√3), using √3 twice (√3 V_L I_L already contains it), taking φ as the 30° line-phase shift, ignoring the minus sign of a reversed wattmeter reading, and adding unbalanced line currents arithmetically to find the neutral current instead of as phasors.

formulas.plainText: P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ = 3 V_ph I_ph cos φ

notes.text: In Nepal the line voltage is 400 V and the phase voltage is 400/√3 ≈ 230 V. When a question says 'a 400 V three-phase supply', 400 V is the line voltage; a 'three-phase 230 V' figure is the phase voltage.

The √3 appears only once: P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ uses line values and P = 3 V_ph I_ph cos φ uses phase values. Writing 3 V_L I_L cos φ or √3 V_ph I_ph cos φ is wrong; both correct forms give the same answer for star and for delta.
φ in the power formulas is the angle between phase voltage and phase current, i.e. the impedance angle of the load — never the 30° between line and phase quantities.

The same impedance draws three times the power and three times the line current in delta as in star from the same supply. Star-delta starters use this to cut the starting current of induction motors to one third.

formulas.title: Star connection
formulas.description: Line and phase relations for a star (Y) connection; the line voltage leads the corresponding phase voltage by 30° and a neutral point exists.

formulas.title: Delta connection
formulas.description: Line and phase relations for a delta (Δ) connection; the line current lags the corresponding phase current by 30° and there is no neutral.

formulas.title: Three-phase active power
formulas.plainText: P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ = 3 V_ph I_ph cos φ
formulas.description: Total active power of a balanced load in watts; φ is the angle between phase voltage and phase current and the formula holds for star and delta.

formulas.title: Three-phase reactive and apparent power
formulas.plainText: Q = √3 V_L I_L sin φ,  S = √3 V_L I_L
formulas.description: Reactive power in VAR and apparent power in VA of a balanced three-phase load; S = √(P² + Q²) and cos φ = P/S.

formulas.title: Two-wattmeter power factor
formulas.description: Power factor angle of a balanced load from the two wattmeter readings W1 and W2; the total power is always W1 + W2.

flashcards.front: In a star connection, how are line and phase quantities related?
flashcards.back: V_L = √3 V_ph (the line voltage leads by 30°) and I_L = I_ph; a neutral point exists, so a 4-wire supply is possible.

flashcards.front: In a delta connection, how are line and phase quantities related?
flashcards.back: V_L = V_ph and I_L = √3 I_ph (the line current lags by 30°); there is no neutral.

flashcards.front: Write the three-phase active power in line and in phase terms.
